summary: A country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa; in 1958 it was the first to become independent from France, it holds the world's richest bauxite reserves, and it is the source of the Niger and other great West African rivers.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam came to Guinea through the trade and scholarly networks of the medieval Mali Empire. In the 1720s Fula Muslims launched a jihad on the Fouta Djallon plateau and founded the Imamate of Futa Jallon, governed by Islamic law; the Wassoulou Empire (1878–1898) founded by Samori Touré in the late 19th century also invoked Islam to resist French colonization. The Fula, Malinke and Susu are therefore almost entirely Muslim, and Islam is the country's main faith.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: At the end of the 19th century France colonized Guinea, and missions such as the Catholic Spiritans came with it; the believers are concentrated mainly in the forest region of the south-east and in the capital Conakry. After independence in 1958, the Sékou Touré regime expelled foreign missionaries in 1967, and in 1970 arrested the Archbishop of Conakry, Raymond-Marie Tchidimbo, on charges of treason and imprisoned him for nearly nine years, so the church's development was for a time set back.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: The Kissi, Guerze (Kpelle) and Toma of the south-eastern forest region preserve ancestral spirit and nature worship, and the "sacred groves" are the sites of initiation and secret society rites. These regions came into contact with Islam later, and traditional beliefs often coexist with Christianity or Islam.

religion.background: The Islamization of Guinea began in the time of the medieval Mali Empire; the Imamate of Futa Jallon in the 18th century and the Samori Empire in the 19th century made Islam the mainstream of the plateau and the interior. French colonization in the 1890s brought Catholicism, but it developed mainly in the forest region and coastal cities. In 1958 Guinea became independent from France under Sékou Touré, whose Marxist regime for a time suppressed religion; religious freedom was restored after 1984, and today Muslims are the overwhelming majority, while the forest region still preserves traditional beliefs and Christianity.

ranking.name: Pular (Fula)
ranking.description: Pular is the language of the Fula people and is spoken mainly on the Fouta Djallon plateau in the center of the country. In the 18th century scholars of the Imamate of Futa Jallon wrote Pular in the Arabic script (known as Ajami) and composed religious poetry, making it one of the few West African indigenous languages with a written tradition. The Fula are the largest ethnic group in Guinea, so Pular has the most speakers.

ranking.name: Maninka
ranking.description: Maninka is spoken in Upper Guinea in the north-east, centered on Kankan, the core area of the Mali Empire founded by Sundiata in the 13th century. In 1949 the Guinean Souleymane Kanté invented the "N'Ko" alphabet, specifically for writing Manding, which became a symbol of the Manding cultural revival.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: In 1891 France established French Guinea, and French became the colonial administrative language. After independence in 1958, Sékou Touré promoted a "cultural revolution" in 1968–1984 with education in eight indigenous languages, but with limited success, and after 1984 schools returned to teaching in French. French is the official language, used mainly in government, higher education and cities, and it has few native speakers.

language.history: The languages of Guinea belong mainly to the Niger–Congo family, divided into Fula, Manding (Maninka, Susu) and, in the forest region, Kissi, Guerze and others. The medieval Mali Empire spread Manding widely, and in the 18th century the Islamic scholars of Futa Jallon wrote Pular in the Arabic script. In the French colonial period French became the administrative language. After independence Sékou Touré's indigenous-language education policy was a rare experiment in Africa; although it was withdrawn after 1984, indigenous languages still dominate radio and daily life today.

ranking.name: Peanut stew
ranking.description: Beef, mutton or chicken stewed with peanut butter, tomato and onion in a thick, rich sauce, often with sweet potato or cabbage added, and eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and were brought to West Africa by Portuguese traders in the 16th century; in the colonial period the French grew them in large quantities as a main cash crop. The Manding and Bambara incorporated peanuts into traditional stews, giving rise to this dish, called "tigadèguèna" in Guinean Maninka. It is popular throughout the West African interior and is a common home-cooked dish for both everyday meals and festivals.

ranking.name: Yassa chicken (lemon-onion chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken is marinated in plenty of onion, lemon juice, mustard and chili, grilled, and then stewed with the onion sauce; the flavor is tangy and appetizing.
ranking.history: Yassa chicken originates in the Casamance region of southern Senegal, a neighboring country, and came to Guinea through cross-border contact between peoples. The use of citrus and mustard reflects ingredients introduced in the colonial period. It is a common dish at Guinean banquets and festivals, and its sourness whets the appetite in the hot climate.

ranking.name: Fonio
ranking.description: An ancient African millet with extremely fine grains, soft and fluffy when cooked, which can be made into porridge, steamed like couscous, or served with stews.
ranking.history: Fonio is one of the oldest cultivated cereals of West Africa, grown there for thousands of years; it is very drought-tolerant, grows in poor soils, and matures quickly, supplying food during the "hungry season" before other crops are harvested. The Fouta Djallon plateau in Guinea is the main production area, and Guinea is the world's largest producer of fonio. It was once regarded as food for the poor, but in recent years it has regained attention for being gluten-free and highly nutritious.

ranking.name: Tomato rice (riz gras)
ranking.description: Rice cooked together with tomato, onion, oil and meat, the grains absorbing the sauce and turning red, often cooked with pieces of meat and vegetables such as cabbage and carrot.
ranking.history: The upper Niger valley is one of the domestication areas of African rice (Oryza glaberrima), rice growing has a long history in Guinea, and Guineans are among the peoples with a high per-capita rice consumption in the world. This oil-rich rice dish shares its origin with the jollof rice of the Wolof of Senegambia and came with regional trade. It is cooked in large quantities at weddings, religious festivals and family gatherings, and is an important dish for hosting guests.

ranking.name: Fufu
ranking.description: Cassava, yam or plantain is boiled and pounded into a soft, elastic dough, eaten with peanut sauce, leaf sauce or palm oil stew.
ranking.history: Pounding starchy dough is a food tradition shared by West and Central Africa, and is especially common in the forest region of Guinea. Cassava is a crop that the Portuguese introduced from the Americas in the 16th century, and it became an important ingredient because of its high yield. People usually pinch off a small piece of fufu in the hand and dip it into the stew, and it represents the typical West African way of eating a starchy staple with a sauce.
